inline.s: “Vow of Transcending the World” refers to the vow spoken earlier: “It shall surpass and excel the lands of countless Buddhas.”
Again, as a great giver I appear, to succor all the poor and distressed; I shall grant every being relief, and give them long nights free from sorrow and care.
I shall bring forth every root of goodness, and accomplish the fruit of bodhi; when I attain perfect enlightenment, my name shall be Immeasurable Life.
“Immeasurable Life” is the Buddha’s name; its transliteration is Amitābha.
When beings hear this name
(when beings hear this name),
all shall come to my land; like the Buddha’s golden body, their wondrous marks shall be complete.
Likewise with a heart of great compassion, benefiting every kind of being,
them
free from desire and deep in right mindfulness, with pure wisdom cultivating the pure life.
“Every kind of being” means sentient beings.
May my light of wisdom shine universally over lands in the ten directions, dispel the gloom of the three defilements, and with clarity rescue all from hardship and adversity.

“Three defilements” is another name for the three poisons, namely greed, anger, and delusion. “The gloom of the three defilements” is the darkness of the three poisons. “With clarity rescue all from hardship and adversity” means using the light of wisdom to rescue beings from all their hardships and adversities.
All shall cast off the suffering of the three paths, and extinguish the darkness of all afflictions; I shall open for them the eye of wisdom, and they shall attain a body of light.

“Three paths” are the path of blood, the path of knives, and the path of fire. The path of blood is the animal realm, because animals constantly dwell where they are killed or devour one another; the path of knives is the realm of hungry ghosts, because hungry ghosts constantly dwell where hunger, or swords, whips, and staves oppress them; the path of fire is the hell realm, because hells constantly dwell in freezing ice or where fierce flames scorch and sear. These three paths are another name for the three evil paths.
Shut
(shut)
all evil paths, and open
(throw open)
the gate of good destinies; for all beings I open the Dharma-store, and broadly bestow the treasure of merit.

“Evil paths”: for ordinary people in the world, the evil paths mean the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. Here the evil paths are the five evil paths spoken of in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) — hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. “Block all evil paths” means cutting off the road of birth-and-death and transmigration. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Each should strive with diligence, and seek deliverance with his own effort. You shall surely transcend and pass beyond, and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Cutting across the five evil paths, the roads of destiny close of themselves.”

“Five evil paths” are: hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Because these five paths are the road of birth-and-death and transmigration, for a cultivator who would end birth-and-death and escape the three realms, all of them are evil paths.
“Good destinies”: here “good destinies” does not mean the three good paths among the six paths (gods, humans, and asuras), but rather the ending of the road of birth-and-death and transmigration.
“For all beings I open the Dharma-store”: teaching beings to reveal their own intrinsic nature (the Dharma-store).

“Dharma-store” is also called the store of Buddha-dharma, or the tathāgatagarbha; that is, the intrinsic nature of sentient beings, which contains and holds all the merits of the Tathāgata’s fruition-ground. (For details, see
Mind, Intrinsic Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
Like the Buddha’s unobstructed wisdom, walking in the practice of compassion, always a teacher of gods and humans, he becomes the hero of the three realms.
Proclaiming the Dharma with the lion’s roar, delivering every sentient being, perfecting all past vows
(perfecting and fulfilling the forty-eight great vows made in the past),
all shall become Buddhas
(causing every being reborn in my land to attain Buddhahood)
“Lion’s roar”: the Buddha proclaims the Dharma without any fear, his voice shakes the ten directions, and all demons are subdued, just as when the lion roars, the hundred beasts submit.
“All shall become Buddhas”: causing every being reborn in my land to attain Buddhahood. That is, as the forty-eight vows spoken of earlier say:

“All sentient beings, including those in the realm of Yama and in the three evil paths, who come to be born in my land and receive my Dharma’s transformation, shall all accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
If this vow is fulfilled
(if this vow is about to be accomplished),
the great thousand worlds shall tremble in response
(the great thousand worlds shall tremble in resonance),
and all the gods of the sky shall rain down rare and wondrous flowers."

"The Buddha told Ānanda: when the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, the entire earth at once quaked in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself, and a voice in the air praised him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment."

The Buddha told Ānanda: when the bhikṣu Dharmākara had spoken this verse, the entire earth immediately quaked in six ways. The heavens rained wondrous flowers, scattering them upon him. Music sounded of itself in the air, praising him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment (he shall certainly become a Buddha).

“Six ways of quaking”: the six signs of auspicious quaking, namely movement, surging, quaking, striking, roaring, and bursting. These six kinds of quaking can be known and seen only by those with the divine eye; ordinary beings know nothing of them. “A voice in the air praised him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment”: because the bhikṣu Dharmākara said in his forty-eight vows that if any one of those vows were not fulfilled, he would not attain Buddhahood. “A voice in the air praised him, saying: he shall certainly attain supreme perfect enlightenment” is a prophecy: the bhikṣu Dharmākara will certainly become a Buddha, and all forty-eight vows will be completely fulfilled.
This chapter tells how the bhikṣu Dharmākara, after cultivating through immeasurable kalpas, accumulated merit and virtue, and thereby evoked the manifestation of a Buddha-land (
“he evoked a vast and pure dwelling-place”
) — the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

“Ānanda, after the bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these vast and lofty vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, and in the midst of the assembly of gods, humans, and the great multitude, he dwelt in true wisdom, advanced with brave and vigorous effort, and single-mindedly devoted himself to adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he cultivated was open and vast, surpassing and uniquely wondrous; once established, it abides forever, without decay or change.”

Ānanda, after the bhikṣu Dharmākara had made these forty-eight great vows before the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja and in the midst of the assembly of gods, humans, and the great multitude, he dwelt in true wisdom and cultivated with brave and vigorous effort, always single-mindedly devoted to cultivating and adorning the wondrous land. The Buddha-land he would cultivate was open and broad, magnificent and vast, surpassing and uniquely wondrous, altogether foremost. It abides forever just so, never decaying or growing old.

“The Buddha-land he cultivated”: the Buddha-land he cultivated was evoked and manifested by the bhikṣu Dharmākara’s immeasurable and boundless fruition-enlightenment and wondrous virtue. The Vajraśekhara Sutra says:
“This Buddha-land alone is entirely accomplished through the purity of vajra intrinsic nature.”

“Once established, it abides forever, without decay or change”: the Buddha-land he cultivated (the Land of Ultimate Bliss), once established, abides forever just so, and has no marks of decay or damage.

“For immeasurable kalpas he accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire, and clung to nothing among forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, tactile objects, or mental objects. He delighted only in recollecting the good roots cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the peaceful practice, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he planted the roots of all virtues, counting no hardship as hardship.”

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated and planted virtuous conduct. He gave rise to no thoughts of greed, anger, delusion, or desire, nor did he cling to the objects of the six dusts. He delighted only in recollecting the good cultivated by the Buddhas of the past. He practiced the peaceful practice, far removed from falsehood. Relying on the gate of ultimate truth, he cultivated the roots of all virtues, counting no hardship or difficulty as hardship.

“Six dusts”: the dust of form, the dust of sound, the dust of fragrance, the dust of taste, the dust of touch, and the dust of mental objects. “Dust” means defilement; it is so called because it can defile the human mind and prevent the true nature from manifesting. They are also called the six objects, being the outer objects perceived by the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind). “Ultimate truth”: the true principle of nirvāṇa’s stillness, seen by sagely wisdom, is called ultimate truth.

“With few desires and contentment, he sought only the pure Dharma, benefiting the multitude of beings. His vow and aspiration never wearied, and his power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he always cherished compassion and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them onward. He revered the Three Jewels and served his teachers, with no heart of falsehood or flattery.”

He had few desires and was content, seeking only good dharmas and benefiting the multitude of beings. His vow and aspiration never wearied, and his power of patience was accomplished. Toward all sentient beings he always cherished compassion and patience. With a gentle countenance and loving words, he exhorted and encouraged them onward. He revered the Three Jewels and served his teachers, with no heart of falsehood or flattery.
“Pure dharmas”: the general name for all good dharmas. “Power of patience”: the power of patient endurance. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Again I see sons of the Buddha dwelling in the power of patience; when arrogant and overbearing people revile and beat them, they can endure it all, in order to seek the Buddha-way.”
“Compassion and patience”: compassion and forbearance. “Exhorted”: admonished and instructed. “Encouraged them onward”: urged them to advance.

“Adorning all practices, his model and demeanor were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded well the karma of speech, never ridiculing the faults of others; he guarded well the karma of body, never transgressing the precepts and deportment; he guarded well the karma of mind, pure and undefiled. Toward all cities, towns, kinsmen, and treasures, he had no attachment whatsoever. Always with giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — the practices of the six pāramitās — he taught and established beings, causing them to dwell in the supreme and true way.”

The bhikṣu Dharmākara adorned all practices, and his model and demeanor were complete. He contemplated all dharmas as illusory, and his samādhi was ever still. He guarded well the karma of speech, never ridiculing the faults of others; he guarded well the karma of body, never transgressing the precepts and deportment; he guarded well the karma of mind, pure and undefiled. Toward all cities, towns, kinsmen, and treasures, he had no attachment whatsoever. Always with the wondrous practices of the six pāramitās — giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom — he taught and established beings, causing them to dwell in the supreme and true way.

“Model and demeanor”: the standard that conduct should follow. “Contemplated all dharmas as illusory”: seeing all dharmas as like illusions. “Precepts and deportment”: precepts are the moral rules, deportment is the proper bearing; these are what a cultivator must follow in conducting himself in the world.

“Because he accomplished such good roots, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response. Sometimes he was a householder or a man of wealth, of noble or honored family; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage emperor; sometimes a lord of the six heavens of desire, or even a Brahmā king. Before all Buddhas he reverently made offerings, never interrupting. Such merit cannot be fully told.”

Because the bhikṣu Dharmākara had accomplished such good roots, wherever he was born, immeasurable treasures naturally welled up. In his successive lives he was sometimes a householder or a man of wealth, of noble or honored family; sometimes a kṣatriya king or a wheel-turning sage king; sometimes the lord of the heavens of the desire realm, or even the great Brahmā king of the form realm. Before all Buddhas he reverently made offerings, never interrupting. Such merit cannot be fully told.

“Immeasurable treasures naturally appeared in response”: because the bhikṣu Dharmākara accumulated over many kalpas the merit of giving and keeping precepts, treasures appeared in response and welled up of themselves. “Householder”: a general term for one who accumulates wealth and possesses virtue. “Kṣatriya”: that is, kṣatriya, the second of India’s four castes. “Four castes”: brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras. Brahmins were the priests of ancient India, holding the highest authority; kṣatriyas were the royal class, honored equally with the brahmins; vaiśyas were the ordinary class of workers, farmers, and merchants; śūdras were slaves made to serve others. “Six heavens of desire”: the desire realm (the world inhabited by beings who have the two desires of sexuality and food) has six levels of heaven, hence the name six heavens of desire: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, and the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations. “Lord of the six heavens of desire”: the lord of each heaven of the desire realm. “Brahmā king”: short for the great Brahmā king. “Form realm”: above the desire realm; because the beings of this realm have only material bodies and are free from the two desires of sexuality and food, it is called the form realm.

“Sometimes the lord of the heavens of the desire realm, or even the great Brahmā king of the form realm”: the Sutra of the Great Vehicle of Immeasurable Life, Spoken by the Buddha (Song translation) says:
“Ānanda, when the bhikṣu who made the vows
(the bhikṣu Dharmākara),

while practicing the bodhisattva path, was before all Buddhas, he was reverent and respectful. He served and made offerings without ever interrupting. As a king of the Four Great Kings, he constantly came before the Buddhas, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, he constantly came before the Buddhas, reverently bowing and making offerings. As a lord of the Yāma Heaven, a lord of the Tuṣita Heaven, a lord of the Heaven of Enjoying Transformations, a lord of the Heaven of Freely Enjoying Others’ Transformations, and even as a great Brahmā king, he constantly came before the Buddhas, reverently bowing and making offerings. ”
“From his body and mouth there constantly came immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like that of candana
(zhān)

and utpala flowers, and its fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his form was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary marks were all complete. From his hands there constantly came endless treasures and adornments, everything needed, the finest of things, bringing benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition, he could cause immeasurable beings to give rise to the aspiration for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Through the response evoked by his merit, from the bhikṣu Dharmākara’s body and mouth there constantly came immeasurable wondrous fragrance, like that of candana and utpala flowers, and its fragrance pervaded immeasurable worlds. Wherever he was born, his form was dignified, and the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary marks were all complete. From his hands there constantly came endless treasures and adornments, everything needed, the finest of things, to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings. By this cause and condition, he could cause immeasurable beings to give rise to the aspiration for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

“Eighty secondary marks” is also called the eighty follow-the-form marks, namely: an invisible crown of the head; a high nose with unseen nostrils; eyebrows like the new moon; earlobes hanging low; a body firm as Nārāyaṇa’s; joints like hooked chains; a body that turns at once like an elephant king; feet that leave prints four inches above the ground when walking; nails the color of red copper, thin and glossy; knee bones firm and perfectly round; a clean body; a soft body; an unbent body; round and slender fingers; hidden and covered finger-lines; deep and unseen veins; unseen ankles; a glossy body; a body that holds itself without bending; a fulfilled body; complete bearing and deportment; a full and perfect bearing; an abode so secure that none can move him; majesty that overawes all; all beings rejoicing at the sight of him; a face neither long nor large; proper features with an unyielding countenance; a full and perfect face and eyes; lips the color of the bimba fruit; a voice deep and far-reaching; a navel deep and perfectly round; hairs curling to the right; fulfilled hands and feet; hands and feet that follow his intent; clear and straight hand-lines; long hand-lines; unbroken hand-lines; all beings of evil mind becoming gentle and joyful at the sight of him; a broad and exceedingly lovely face; a face as pure and full as the moon; speaking gently and joyfully according to the minds of beings; fragrance issuing from his pores; supreme fragrance issuing from his mouth; a bearing like the lion’s; advancing and resting like an elephant king; a gait like the goose king’s; a head like the mādhava fruit; a voice complete in every part; four teeth white and sharp; a red tongue; a thin tongue; red hairs; soft and clean hairs; broad and long eyes; the marks of the gate of death complete; hands and feet red and white like the color of lotus flowers; an unseen navel; an unseen belly; a slender belly; a body that does not lean or move; a body that bears weight; a large body; a tall body; hands and feet soft, clean, smooth, and glossy; a halo extending ten feet on all four sides; light shining as he walks; looking upon beings with impartiality; never slighting beings; voice that neither increases nor decreases with the voices of beings; teaching the Dharma without attachment; teaching the Dharma according to the language of beings; a voice that responds to beings; teaching the Dharma in sequence according to causes and conditions; all beings finding his marks inexhaustible to behold; beholding him without ever being satiated; long and lovely hair; hair never disheveled; hair curled in a lovely whorl; hair the color of blue pearls; hands and feet bearing the marks of virtue.

“The Buddha told Ānanda: the bhikṣu Dharmākara cultivated the bodhisattva path, accumulating merit and virtue beyond measure or bound. In all dharmas he attained freedom, which is not something that verbal discrimination can know. The vows he made were perfectly accomplished, and he truly abides in a pure Buddha-land complete in adornment, majestic in virtue, vast and great.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: the bhikṣu Dharmākara cultivated the bodhisattva path, accumulating merit and virtue beyond measure or bound. In all dharmas he attained freedom; this is not something that verbal discrimination can know. The forty-eight great vows he made were perfectly accomplished, and he truly abides in a pure Buddha-land complete in adornment, majestic in virtue, vast and great.

“When Ānanda heard what the Buddha said, he addressed the World-Honored One: the Bodhisattva Dharmākara who attained bodhi — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a present Buddha now dwelling in another world?”

When Ānanda heard what the Buddha said, he addressed the World-Honored One: the Bodhisattva Dharmākara who attained Buddhahood — is he a Buddha of the past? A Buddha of the future? Or a present Buddha dwelling in another world?

“The World-Honored One told him: that Buddha Tathāgata, in coming has nowhere he comes from, in going has nowhere he goes; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is not past, present, or future. But to repay his vows and save beings, he now appears in the west, ten billion Buddha-lands from here, in a world named Ultimate Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since his attainment of Buddhahood. He now teaches the Dharma, surrounded with reverence by immeasurable and countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.”

The World-Honored One told Ānanda: that Buddha Tathāgata (Amitābha Buddha), in coming has nowhere he comes from, in going has nowhere he goes; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is neither a Buddha of the past, nor a Buddha of the present, nor a Buddha of the future. But to repay his vows and broadly save beings,
he now appears in the west, ten billion Buddha-lands from here,

in a world named Ultimate Bliss. Dharmākara became a Buddha, with the name Amitābha. Ten kalpas have passed since his attainment of Buddhahood. He now teaches the Dharma, surrounded with reverence by immeasurable and countless multitudes of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas.

“That Buddha Tathāgata, in coming has nowhere he comes from, in going has nowhere he goes; he is neither born nor extinguished, and is not past, present, or future”: this is the ultimate truth, spoken with respect to the true mark of all dharmas.
“He now appears in the west, ten billion Buddha-lands from here”: the assembled Sutra of Immeasurable Life Tathāgata (Tang translation) says:

“The Buddha told Ānanda: to the west of here, ten billion Buddha-lands away, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. The bhikṣu Dharmākara attained Buddhahood there, with the name Immeasurable Life, and now teaches the Dharma.”
The Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:

“The Buddha told the elder Śāriputra: passing from here to the west through ten billion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Ultimate Bliss. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who now teaches the Dharma.”
“Ten kalpas have passed since his attainment of Buddhahood”: the Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Ānanda asked the Buddha: did the Bodhisattva Dharmākara already become a Buddha and then enter extinction? Or has he not yet become a Buddha? Or is he now present? The Buddha told Ānanda: the Bodhisattva Dharmākara has now become a Buddha; he is present in the west, ten billion lands from here, and his Buddha-world is named Peace and Bliss. Ānanda asked again: how long has it been since that Buddha attained the way? The Buddha said: since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed.”
The Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:
“Ten kalpas have passed since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood.”

“The Buddha told how Amitābha Buddha, while a bodhisattva, sought and attained these vows. At that time Prince Ajātaśatru, together with five hundred great householders, heard it and were all greatly delighted. Each took a golden flower-canopy and came before the Buddha to pay homage. After offering the flower-canopies to the Buddha, they withdrew and sat to one side to hear the sutra, and in their minds they vowed: when we become Buddhas, may we all be like Amitābha Buddha.”

When the World-Honored One proclaimed how Amitābha Buddha, while a bodhisattva, perfected and accomplished the forty-eight great vows through accumulating merit and virtue, at that time Prince Ajātaśatru, together with five hundred great householders, heard it and were all greatly delighted. Each took a golden flower-canopy and came together before the Buddha to pay homage. After offering the flower-canopies to the Buddha, they sat to one side to hear the sutra, and in their minds they made this vow: when we become Buddhas, may we all be as wondrous as Amitābha Buddha.

“The Buddha knew it at once, and told the monks: this prince and the others shall become Buddhas hereafter. In former lives they dwelt on the bodhisattva path, and for countless kalpas they made offerings to four billion Buddhas. At the time of Buddha Kāśyapa they were my disciples; now they make offerings to me, and so we meet again. Then all the monks who heard the Buddha’s words rejoiced on their behalf.”

The World-Honored One knew at once the vow in their minds, and told the monks: Prince Ajātaśatru and the five hundred great householders shall become Buddhas hereafter. In former lives they dwelt on the bodhisattva path, and for countless kalpas they made offerings to four billion Buddhas. At the time of Buddha Kāśyapa they were my disciples; today they come to make offerings to me, and so we meet again. Then all the monks who heard the Buddha’s words rejoiced on their behalf.

blocks.text: 2. The Land and the Beings of Ultimate Bliss

inline.s: “The land and the beings of Ultimate Bliss”: the dependent reward and the direct reward of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. “Direct reward”: the body and mind of sentient beings, the principal fruit-body evoked by past karmic causes. “Dependent reward”: the fruit-reward on which body and mind depend for dwelling, such as lands, great earths, houses, and implements — that is, the conditions of life.
“The land adorned and pure”: the land
is adorned and pure.

“The Buddha said to Ānanda: that realm of Ultimate Bliss has immeasurable merit and is complete in adornment. It is forever without even the names of myriad sufferings, hardships, evil destinies, or the afflictions of demons. It has none of the differences of the four seasons, cold and heat, rain and gloom. It has no great or small rivers and seas, no hills or hollows, no thorns or gravel, no iron-ring mountains, Sumeru, or mountains of earth and stone. Only the seven treasures and gold, all natural, form its ground, broad, level, and upright, without limit or bound. Subtle, wondrous, rare, and beautiful, pure and adorned, it surpasses all worlds of the ten directions.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: the Land of Ultimate Bliss has immeasurable merit and is complete in adornment. It is forever without even the names of myriad sufferings, hardships (the eight difficulties), evil paths (the three evil paths), or the afflictions of demons (if even the names do not exist, then such things certainly do not occur). It has none of the differences of the four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, and winter), cold and heat, or rain and gloom (rainy days and overcast days). Still less has it great or small rivers, lakes, and seas, hills and hollows, thorns and gravel, or mountains made of iron-ring mountains, Sumeru, and earth and stone. It is entirely grounded in the seven treasures and gold, all natural, broad, level, and upright, boundless and limitless. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is subtle, wondrous, rare, and beautiful, pure and adorned, surpassing all worlds of the ten directions.

“Myriad sufferings”: all kinds of suffering. By classification there are three sufferings, eight sufferings, ten sufferings, and one hundred and ten sufferings. “Three sufferings”: the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioning. First, the suffering of suffering: beings in the world, already suffering by having a body subject to birth and death, are pressed and scorched by further sufferings, so that suffering is added to suffering; this is called the suffering of suffering. Second, the suffering of change: the suffering felt when a state of happiness that appears only occasionally is once lost. Third, the suffering of conditioning: the suffering of all formations being impermanent, flowing on without cease, and never able to abide in peace. “Eight sufferings”: first, the suffering of birth, the pain at the time of being born; second, the suffering of old age, the pain of years and bodily weakness; third, the suffering of illness, the pain at the time of sickness; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the time of dying; fifth, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the pain of parting from what one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting the hated, the pain of being together with enemies; seventh, the suffering of not getting what one seeks, the pain of desires unfulfilled; eighth, the suffering of the raging five aggregates, the pain of the illusory body and mind of the five aggregates (form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness) giving rise to delusion and creating karma amid the objects of the six dusts, and being scorched and seared like a blazing fire with no rest. “The ten sufferings and the one hundred and ten sufferings”: as to the ten sufferings and the one hundred and ten sufferings, Master Lianchi’s Commentary and Notes on the Amitābha Sutra Spoken by the Buddha says:

“As for the ten sufferings, the Sutra of the Bodhisattva Collection says: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; and so on up to tenth, the suffering of birth-and-death and transmigration. As for the one hundred and ten sufferings, the Yogācārabhūmi says: first, the suffering of undifferentiated transmigration; second, the suffering of desire; third, the suffering of delusion; and so on up to the fifty-fifth suffering; then nine kinds of suffering, and within those nine, further opened out in turn to make fifty-five, which together make one hundred and ten sufferings.”

“Eight difficulties”: eight places and situations in which one is hindered from seeing and hearing the Buddhadharma, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, the continent of Uttarakuru, the Heaven of No Perception, being blind, deaf, or mute, worldly intelligence and clever argument, and before a Buddha’s appearance or after a Buddha’s nirvāṇa. Among these, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals belong to the three evil paths; because their karmic obstruction is too heavy, it is very hard for them to see and hear the Buddhadharma. People of Uttarakuru have great blessings, but they do not know the Buddhadharma, and so cannot end birth-and-death. The Heaven of No Perception is a place where non-Buddhists are born, and the people there likewise cannot end birth-and-death. One afflicted with blindness, deafness, or muteness naturally cannot see or hear the Buddhadharma. Worldly intelligence and clever argument means people of the world relying on their petty cleverness, unwilling to cultivate with a humble mind, and even slandering the Buddhadharma. Being born before a Buddha’s appearance in the world or after a Buddha’s nirvāṇa, one can neither see the Buddha nor hear the Buddhadharma.

“Afflictions of demons”: the harm done by demons (the four demons). “Four demons”: the demon of afflictions, the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of death, and the demon of heaven. The demon of afflictions means that habits such as greed, anger, and delusion can afflict body and mind; the demon of the five aggregates means that the five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formation, and consciousness can produce all suffering; the demon of death means that death can cut off the root of a person’s life; the demon of heaven means heavenly demons and non-Buddhists who can ruin people’s good works. “Sumeru”: rendered in Chinese as Wondrous High Mountain, the center of a small world. This mountain is made of the four treasures of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; no other mountain can compare with its height, and it is the king of mountains. “Iron-ring mountains”: the iron mountains that encircle the salty sea and mark off a small world. “Seven treasures”: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, amber, fine jade, and carnelian.
“When Ānanda heard this, he addressed the World-Honored One: if that land has no Sumeru, on what do the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three depend for dwelling?”

When Ānanda heard this, he reverently asked the World-Honored One: if the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no Sumeru, then on what do the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three depend for dwelling?

“On what do they depend for dwelling”: in ordinary Buddha-lands the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is on the slopes of Sumeru and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is on its summit; both depend on the mountain for dwelling. Ānanda heard the Buddha say that the Land of Ultimate Bliss has no Sumeru, and so asked this question.
“The Buddha told Ānanda: the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and even all the heavens of the form and formless realms — on what do they depend for dwelling?”
The Buddha asked Ānanda in return: the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and all the heavens of the form realm and formless realm — none of them is on Sumeru, so on what do they depend for dwelling?

“All the heavens, on what do they depend for dwelling”: the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three dwell depending on Sumeru, and are called earth-dwelling heavens; all the heavens from the Yāma Heaven upward dwell in space, and are called space-dwelling heavens.
“Ānanda said: it is brought about by inconceivable karmic power.”
Ānanda reverently replied: they dwell in space; this is brought about by inconceivable karmic power.
“Inconceivable”: beyond what the thought and speech of sentient beings can reach.

“The Buddha said to Ānanda: the inconceivable karma — can you know it? Your own fruit-reward is inconceivable; the karmic reward of beings is also inconceivable; the good roots of beings are inconceivable; the sage power of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. The beings of that land, by their merit and power of goodness, dwell on the ground of practice and karma, and by the Buddha’s spiritual power, are able to be thus.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: the inconceivable karma — can you know it? Your own fruit-reward is inconceivable; the karmic reward of beings is also inconceivable; the good roots of beings are inconceivable; the sage power of the Buddhas and the worlds of the Buddhas are also inconceivable. Because the beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, by their merit and power of goodness, dwell on the ground of Amitābha Buddha’s practice and karma, and by the spiritual power of Amitābha Buddha, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are able to dwell depending on space.
“The ground of practice and karma”: the ground accomplished by Amitābha Buddha’s great vows, great practice, and great karma.

“Ānanda said: the karmic causes and fruits of karma are inconceivable! Concerning this Dharma, I truly have no doubt. It is only to cut the net of doubt for beings of the future that I asked this question.”

Ānanda said to the Buddha: the karmic causes and fruits of karma are inconceivable! As to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-Three in the Land of Ultimate Bliss being able to dwell depending on space, I truly have no doubt at all. It is only to cut the doubt of beings of the future (since beings of the future might raise this very question) that I asked this question.

“The Buddha told Ānanda: Amitābha Buddha’s majestic spiritual light is the most honored and foremost; the Buddhas of the ten directions cannot equal it. It shines everywhere over Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the east, and likewise in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below. As for the transformed halo on his crown, it may extend one, two, three, or four yojanas, or a hundred, thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million yojanas. The light of other Buddhas may illumine one or two Buddha-lands, or a hundred or a thousand Buddha-lands. Only Amitābha Buddha’s light shines everywhere over immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: Amitābha Buddha’s majestic spiritual light is the most honored and foremost; the Buddhas of the ten directions cannot equal it. The halo on his crown shines everywhere over Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the east, and over Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the south, west, and north, as well as in the four intermediate directions (southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast), above, and below. The crown halos of other Buddhas may shine one, two, three, or four yojanas, or a hundred, thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million yojanas; or they may shine over one or two Buddha-lands, or a hundred or a thousand Buddha-lands. Only Amitābha Buddha’s light shines everywhere over immeasurable, boundless, countless Buddha-lands.
“Halo on his crown”: Buddhas and bodhisattvas have body light and crown light; “halo on his crown” means the crown light
the circular light on the top of the head). The Sutra of Amitāyus, the Buddha of the Threefold Enlightenment, the Towering Buddha, and Deliverance of Humankind (Wu translation) says:

“Amitābha Buddha’s light is the most honored, the foremost without equal. The light of all Buddhas cannot reach it. Amid the countless Buddhas of the eight directions, above and below, there is a Buddha whose crown light shines seven zhang. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines one li. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines two li. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines five li. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines ten li.

There is a Buddha whose crown light shines six million li. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines one Buddha-land. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines two Buddha-lands. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines four Buddha-lands. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines eight Buddha-lands. There is a Buddha whose crown light shines fifteen Buddha-lands.
There is a Buddha whose crown light shines two million Buddha-lands.”
It also says:
“The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Ajita: the light in Amitābha Buddha’s crown is a light of utmost greatness.”
Yojana

is the unit by which India measures distance. There are three kinds, great, medium, and small: the great yojana is about eighty li; the medium yojana is about sixty li; the small yojana is about forty li.

“How far the light of the Buddhas shines depends on the greatness or smallness of the vows and merit they sought and made in former lives when seeking the way. When they become Buddhas, each obtains accordingly. It is what is accomplished of itself, and cannot be calculated in advance.”

How far the light of the Buddhas shines depends on the differences in the greatness or smallness of the original vows and merit with which they sought the way in former lives. When they become Buddhas, each obtains accordingly. This is the natural accomplishment of vow, practice, and karma, and cannot be calculated in advance.

“Amitābha Buddha’s light is excellent and good, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million times. He is the most honored amid lights, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Immeasurable Life Buddha is also named Immeasurable Light Buddha, and also named Boundless Light Buddha, Unobstructed Light Buddha, Unequaled Light Buddha, and also named Light of Wisdom, Ever-Shining Light, Pure Light, Light of Joy, Light of Liberation, Light of Peace and Stability, Light Surpassing the Sun and Moon, and Inconceivable Light.”

Amitābha Buddha’s light is exceedingly beautiful, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon by a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million times; he is the most honored amid lights, the king of Buddhas. Therefore Amitābha Buddha (Immeasurable Life Buddha) is also named Immeasurable Light Buddha, and also named Boundless Light Buddha, Unobstructed Light Buddha, Unequaled Light Buddha, and also named Light of Wisdom, Ever-Shining Light, Pure Light, Light of Joy, Light of Liberation, Light of Peace and Stability, Light Surpassing the Sun and Moon, and Inconceivable Light.
“The most honored amid lights, the king of Buddhas”: the Sutra of Amitāyus, the Buddha of the Threefold Enlightenment, the Towering Buddha, and Deliverance of Humankind (Wu translation) says:
“Amitābha Buddha’s light is beautiful, surpassing the brightness of the sun and moon a hundred, thousand, ten thousand, a hundred million times.
He is the king among all Buddhas, the most honored among lights.”
“Amitābha Buddha (Immeasurable Life Buddha)”: Immeasurable Life Buddha is Amitābha Buddha. Amitābha is a transliteration of the Sanskrit, while Immeasurable Life is a translation of its meaning.

“Such light shines everywhere over all worlds of the ten directions. Whatever beings encounter this light have their defilements extinguished and goodness born in them, and their bodies and minds become gentle. If they are in the places of utmost suffering of the three paths, seeing this light they all find rest, and at the end of life all attain liberation. If there are beings who hear of the majestic virtue of his light, and day and night proclaim it with an undivided mind, they shall be born in that land according to their wish.”
Such

light shines everywhere over all worlds of the ten directions. If there are beings who encounter this light, their evil defilements are extinguished and good roots are born in them, and their bodies (actions) and minds (thoughts) become gentle. If they are in the places of utmost suffering of the three evil paths and see this light, all their pain and torment come to rest, and at the end of life all attain liberation. If there are beings who hear of the majestic virtue of his light, and day and night proclaim it with an undivided mind, they shall be born in that land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss) according to their wish.
“Immeasurable lifespan and multitude”: the beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss have immeasurable lifespans, and their number is also immeasurable.

“The Buddha said to Ānanda: Immeasurable Life Buddha’s lifespan is long and cannot be reckoned. There are also countless multitudes of śrāvakas, whose spiritual wisdom is penetrating and whose majestic power is free and unhindered, able to hold all worlds in the palm of the hand.”

The Buddha said to Ānanda: Amitābha Buddha’s lifespan is long and cannot be measured or reckoned. There are also countless multitudes of śrāvakas, whose spiritual wisdom is penetrating and whose majestic power is free and unhindered, able to hold all worlds in the palm of the hand.
“Able to hold all worlds in the palm of the hand”: the Vimalakīrti Sutra says:
“A bodhisattva may place the beings of one Buddha-land on his right palm. He flies to the ten directions, showing them everywhere, without moving from his original place.”
The sages of Ultimate Bliss likewise possess such inconceivable majestic virtue.

“Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual powers; all the stars and beings of the three thousand great thousand worlds he knows in number within a single day and night. Suppose the beings of the ten directions all became pratyekabuddhas, each with a lifespan of ten thousand billion years, and all with spiritual powers like Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s. Exhausting their lifespans and their wisdom, reckoning together, the number of śrāvakas in that Buddha’s assembly would not come to one part in ten million.”

Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in spiritual powers; all the stars and beings of the three thousand great thousand worlds, counted through a single day and night, he knows entirely in number. Suppose the beings of the worlds of the ten directions all became pratyekabuddhas, each with a lifespan of ten thousand billion years, and all with spiritual powers like Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s. Exhausting their lifespans and their wisdom, reckoning together the number of śrāvakas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they would still not count out one part in ten million.
“Stars”:
the Sutra of Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment (Han translation) says:
“The Buddha said: ‘And my second disciple, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, flew over the four continents, and in one day and one night counted all the stars, knowing how many there were.”

“Suppose, for example, that the great sea is deep and wide beyond bound. Suppose one takes a single hair and splits it into a hundred parts, so that it is broken as fine as motes of dust. With one such hair-mote, one dips up a drop of the sea — which is more, that drop of water on the hair-mote, or the sea? Ānanda, the number known by Maudgalyāyana and the others is like the water on the hair-mote, while what is not known is like the water of the great sea. The lifespan of that Buddha, and the lifespans of the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans, are likewise: not something that reckoning or analogy can know.”

Suppose, for example, that the great sea is deep and wide beyond bound. Suppose one takes a single hair and splits it into a hundred parts, each part as fine and broken as a mote of dust. With a hair as fine and broken as a dust-mote, one dips up a drop of sea water: how does the water on it compare with the water of the whole great sea? Ānanda, the number counted by those pratyekabuddhas with powers like Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s, through all ten thousand billion years, is like the water on the hair-mote, while the number not yet counted is like the water of the whole great sea. The lifespan of Amitābha Buddha, and the lifespans of the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, gods, and humans of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, are likewise: not something that reckoning or analogy can know.
The above explains: Amitābha Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable, the number of beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is immeasurable, and their lifespans are likewise immeasurable.

“In that Tathāgata’s land there are many jewel trees. There are trees of pure gold, trees of pure silver, trees of lapis lazuli, trees of crystal, trees of amber, trees of fine jade, trees of carnelian, each made of a single treasure and not mixed with other treasures. Or there are those made of two treasures, three treasures, and up to seven treasures, combined in turn. The roots, stems, branches, and trunks are made of one treasure, while the flowers, leaves, and fruits are transformed from other treasures.”

In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are very many jewel trees. There are trees of pure gold, trees of pure silver, trees of pure lapis lazuli, trees of pure crystal, trees of pure amber, trees of pure fine jade, and trees of pure carnelian; each is made of a single treasure alone, not mixed with other treasures. There are also trees made of two treasures, three treasures, and up to seven treasures, combined in turn. The roots, stems, branches, and trunks of these trees are made of one treasure, while the flowers, leaves, and fruits are transformed from other treasures.

“Or there are jewel trees with gold for roots, silver for trunks, lapis lazuli for branches, crystal for tips, amber for leaves, fine jade for flowers, and carnelian for fruits. The remaining trees are again made of the seven treasures, mutually serving as roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, variously combined.”

Or there are jewel trees with gold for roots, silver for trunks, lapis lazuli for branches, crystal for tips, amber for leaves, fine jade for flowers, and carnelian for fruits. The remaining trees are again made of the seven treasures, these jewels mutually serving as roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits, combined together.

“Each in its own row, row matching row, stem facing stem, branches and leaves turned toward one another, flowers and fruits each in place, their glorious colors and radiance too much to behold. When a pure breeze rises from time to time, it gives forth the five tones, subtle and wondrous gong and shang, naturally harmonizing. Such jewel trees are everywhere throughout that land.”

All these jewel trees are arranged in rows each according to its kind, orderly and neat, stem facing stem, branches and leaves turned toward one another, fresh flowers and ripe fruits each in the finest position, brilliantly colorful, bright and lovely, a beauty too much to take in. When a pure breeze blows from time to time, it gives forth exceedingly wondrous music, whose tones and melodies naturally answer one another. Such various jewel trees fill the whole Land of Ultimate Bliss.

“Five tones”: the five notes gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu of the Chinese five-tone scale. “Subtle and wondrous gong and shang”: here “gong and shang” stand for the five tones of gong, shang, jue, zhi, and yu.

“Moreover, at that site of enlightenment there is a bodhi tree, four million li high. Its trunk is five thousand yojanas around, and its branches and leaves spread out two hundred thousand li in the four directions. All the myriad treasures naturally compose it. Its flowers and fruits bloom in splendor, and its radiance shines everywhere. There are also red, green, blue, and white maṇi jewels, kings among treasures, forming its garlands. Cloud-Gathering Treasure locks adorn all its jeweled pillars. Gold, pearls, bells, and chimes
duó
hang all around among its branches.”

Moreover, at the site of enlightenment in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there is a bodhi tree, four million li high. The trunk is five thousand yojanas around (its outer circumference), and its branches and leaves spread out two hundred thousand li. This tree is naturally composed of all the myriad treasures. Its fresh flowers and ripe fruits flourish in brightness, and its radiance shines everywhere. There are also many red, green, blue, and white wish-fulfilling maṇi jewels of various colors; they are kings among treasures and form its garlands. Hooked and linked structures of Cloud-Gathering Treasure adorn all its jeweled pillars. Gold, pearls, and wind-bells hang everywhere among the branches of the bodhi tree.

“Site of enlightenment”: the place where one studies and cultivates the way. “Maṇi jewel”: the wish-fulfilling jewel. “Garlands”: ornaments strung of pearls and jade. “Cloud-Gathering Treasure lock (suǒ)”: a hooked and linked structure made of Cloud-Gathering Treasure. “Cloud-Gathering” is the name of a treasure. The Assembled Sutra of Immeasurable Life Tathāgata (Tang translation) says:
“There are lion, cloud-gathering, and other treasures, which serve as its locks, adorning all its jeweled pillars.”
“Lock (suǒ)” here means a hooked and interlocking structure in a building. “Bells and chimes (
duó
)” are wind-bells hung on buildings.

“Rare and wondrous jeweled nets spread over it. A hundred thousand colors mutually adorn one another, and immeasurable light and flame shine without limit. All adornments appear according to what is fitting. A gentle breeze moves slowly, blowing through the branches and leaves, and performs immeasurable wondrous Dharma-sounds. That sound spreads abroad throughout all Buddha-lands. Clear, flowing, plaintive, and bright, subtle, wondrous, harmonious, and elegant, among the sounds of the worlds of the ten directions it is the foremost.”

Rare and wondrous jeweled nets are spread over the bodhi tree. Each jewel, in a hundred thousand colors, mutually adorns the others, and immeasurable light shines without limit. All adornments appear according to what is fitting. A gentle breeze moves slowly, blowing through the branches and leaves, and performs immeasurable wondrous Dharma-sounds. That sound spreads abroad throughout the Buddha-land (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss). Clear, flowing, plaintive, and bright, subtle, wondrous, harmonious, and elegant, among the sounds of the worlds of the ten directions it is the foremost.
“Each jewel, in a hundred thousand colors”: the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says:
“Each jewel has a thousand lights. Each light has eighty-four thousand colors.”
“Without limit”: without bound. “Throughout all Buddha-lands”: throughout the Buddha-land. Here “all” is the elided sound of “of it.” For example: “cast them to the tail of the Bohai Sea.” (Liezi
Tang Wen) “Plaintive and bright”: plaintive, sweet, and bright.

“If there are beings who behold the bodhi tree, hear its sound, smell its fragrance, taste the flavor of its fruit, touch its light and shadow, or recollect the tree’s merit, they all attain clarity of the six faculties, free from all affliction and trouble, and dwell in non-regression until they attain the Buddha-way. Moreover, by seeing that tree, they obtain three kinds of patience: first, the patience of sound; second, the patience of gentle compliance; third, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.”

If there are beings who see the bodhi tree (eye), hear its sound (ear), smell its fragrance (nose), taste the flavor of its fruit (tongue), touch its light and shadow (body), or recollect the merit of the bodhi tree (mind), they all attain clarity of the six faculties (pure and transparent), free from all affliction and trouble, and dwell securely in the stage of non-regression until they attain Buddhahood. Moreover, by seeing the bodhi tree, they obtain three kinds of patience: first, the patience of sound; second, the patience of gentle compliance; third, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.

“Six faculties”: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. “Patience”: the wisdom-mind abiding in the right Dharma, not dragged about by objects and conditions; this is called patience. “Patience of sound”: awakening through sound to the truth that all dharmas are nonexistent yet appear, and thereby taming one’s mind so as to “not grasp at marks, and abide unmoved in suchness.” “All dharmas are nonexistent yet appear”: all dharmas are illusory marks, like things in a dream, and are not truly existent. (For details, see
The True Mark of All Dharmas

) “Patience of gentle compliance”: meeting objects and conditions, one need not tame one’s mind, but naturally “does not grasp at marks, and abides unmoved in suchness.” At such a time the mind is gentle, good, and compliant. “Patience of the non-arising of dharmas,” abbreviated as the patience of non-arising, is the thorough understanding that all dharmas are originally unborn; sentient and insentient alike are produced by conditions and have no intrinsic nature, and in themselves are empty; thus one abides in the Dharma of non-arising without the mind moving. “No intrinsic nature”: nature means essence; all dharmas have no substantial entity (and so are illusory marks), which is called having no intrinsic nature. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Knowing that all dharmas are always without nature.”
The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“All illusions become natureless.”

“The Buddha told Ānanda: in such a Buddha-land, the flowers, fruits, trees, and woods all do the Buddha’s work for the beings. All this is by the power of Immeasurable Life Buddha’s majestic spirit, by the power of his original vows, by his fulfilled vows, and by his clear, firm, and ultimate vows.”

The Buddha told Ānanda: the Land of Ultimate Bliss is thus supremely wondrous; its flowers, fruits, trees, and woods all teach and transform all beings. All this is by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s majestic spirit, by the power of his original vows, by his fulfilled vows, and by his clear vows, firm vows, and ultimate vows.

“Fulfilled vows”: vows that have been perfectly accomplished. “Clear, firm, and ultimate vows”: the clear vow, the firm vow, and the ultimate vow. The Sutra of Immeasurable Life (Wei translation) says:

“Ānanda! If the gods and humans of that land see this tree, they obtain three kinds of Dharma-patience: first, the patience of sound; second, the patience of gentle compliance; third, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. All this
(all this is)
by the power of Immeasurable Life Buddha’s majestic spirit, by the power of his original vows, by his fulfilled vows, by his clear vows, by his firm vows, and by his ultimate vows.”
“Clear vows”:
vows that are truly clear.
